news.headline: MapQuest Hits No. 1 on App Store After Refusing to Rename Lake Ontario
news.summary: トランプ大統領令に従ってGoogleとAppleがオンタリオ湖を「レイク・アメリカ」に改名する中、MapQuestが改名を拒否したことで話題となり、App Storeで無料アプリ1位に急浮上した。

commentary: 矛盾: テクノロジーの最先端を走るGoogleとAppleが政府の地名変更に即座に従い、「時代遅れ」と思われていたMapQuestが唯一抵抗したことで、デジタル独立心の象徴になってしまった。
滑稽さ: 2026年に人々がMapQuestをダウンロードしている理由が「地図が使いやすいから」ではなく「湖の名前へのこだわり」というのが、もはや完全に別競技。
日本・海外から見ると: 米国の巨大テック企業が大統領令ひとつでカナダとの国境湖の名前を書き換える一方、生き残りをかけたMapQuestが抵抗するという構図、「どっちが体制側か」が完全に逆転している。
imagePrompts: A dusty, cobweb-covered MapQuest logo trophy sitting on a podium labeled '#1 App Store', flanked by glossy Google Maps and Apple Maps trophies with their heads bowed
A giant lake with a name tag that reads 'Lake Ontario / Lake America' — the name half-crossed out, half-reinstated, with a small MapQuest flag planted on the shore
A smartphone screen showing the App Store top chart: #1 MapQuest, #2 ChatGPT — a user staring at the phone with wide, confused eyes, a printed MapQuest direction sheet sticking out of their pocket
captions: MapQuest just beat ChatGPT on the charts. Not by being smarter. Not by being faster. By refusing to rename a lake.
Google built a trillion-dollar company around 'Don't be evil.' Renaming Lake Ontario took, what, an afternoon?
People downloaded MapQuest in 2026. For the lake names. I'm not saying the timeline is broken, but—
Somewhere a MapQuest engineer is reading this news and thinking, 'We've been ready for this moment since 2003.'
You know things are weird when the most principled tech company of the week still gives you seventeen-page directions for a left turn.
captionsJa: MapQuestがApp StoreでChatGPTを抜いた。頭がいいから？いや。湖の名前を変えなかっただけ。
Googleは「悪にならない」を掲げて1兆ドル企業になった。オンタリオ湖の改名は……まあ、午後一本で終わったんでしょうね。
2026年にMapQuestをダウンロードしてる人たちの理由が「湖の名前へのこだわり」って、もうそれ別の何かじゃないですか。
どこかのMapQuestのエンジニア、今ごろ「2003年からずっとこの瞬間を待ってた」って思ってますよ絶対。
一番気骨のあるテック企業が、左折するのに17ページの道案内を出してくるやつっていうのが、今週の話。
candidates.newsEn: MapQuest, the once-dominant mapping service many had assumed was defunct, shot to the top of Apple's App Store free downloads chart after announcing it would keep traditional lake names rather than comply with a Trump executive order renaming Lake Ontario. The company's refusal placed it above ChatGPT on the charts. Google Maps and Apple Maps both updated their labels to reflect the new government-mandated name.

ironyEn.contradiction: Google and Apple — companies that built empires on the idea of organizing the world's information — updated a lake's name on government request faster than they update their own privacy policies.
ironyEn.absurdity: MapQuest, a service people use primarily by accident when their phone dies, is now the symbol of digital resistance.
ironyEn.outside: From outside the U.S., watching Silicon Valley giants rename a Great Lake while a 2005-era mapping app holds the line is a very specific kind of performance art.

ironyEn.contradiction: The boldest act of corporate independence this week came from a company whose main claim to fame is printing out seventeen pages of directions for a twelve-minute drive.
ironyEn.absurdity: It beat ChatGPT. The AI that can write your novel, pass the bar exam, and compose a sonnet — lost the download race to MapQuest over a lake.
ironyEn.outside: Canada's version of Apple Maps still says Lake Ontario, which means the lake is currently named differently depending on which side of the border your iPhone thinks you're on.

news.headline: House Censures Rep. Chuck Edwards for 'Inappropriate Conduct' Toward Female Aides
news.summary: 下院は倫理委員会の調査を受け、ノースカロライナ州選出の共和党議員チャック・エドワーズを、若い女性スタッフ2人への「不適切な行為」を理由に公式に非難決議した。

commentary: 矛盾: 同じ週に下院が「反社会主義決議」を超党派で通過させる一方、職場ハラスメントの議員への非難決議もまた超党派で通過させたという事実が、アメリカ政治の優先順位表を静かに照らし出している。
滑稽さ: 「非難決議」を受けても議員を即座に失職させる仕組みがない。公式に「これはダメ」と書いた紙を渡して、そのまま一緒に仕事を続けるという制度設計が、職場研修のロールプレイより機能していない。
日本・海外から見ると: 非難決議（censure）に法的拘束力がない点は日本でも同じだが、「議会で同僚に紙を渡す」ことが最大の処分というのは、有権者の目にどう映っているのか気になるところ。
imagePrompts: A congressman standing in a grand congressional chamber receiving a formally framed piece of paper labeled 'CENSURE', holding it with both hands while colleagues give a polite golf clap, all returning immediately to their desks
An office bulletin board with a printed 'CENSURE NOTICE' pinned next to a 'EMPLOYEE OF THE MONTH' plaque, both hanging in the same ornate congressional hallway
A giant official government seal stamp reading 'BAD BEHAVIOR CONFIRMED' pressed onto a document, next to a second stamp reading 'STILL IN OFFICE'
captions: Congress officially told him his behavior was unacceptable. He still has his desk. His vote. His parking spot. But they told him.
A censure is basically Congress writing 'we are not pleased' in calligraphy and handing it over at a podium. Very fancy. Completely toothless.
The good news: it was bipartisan. The bad news: the bipartisan consensus was 'yes, this happened' and nothing else.
Most offices call HR. Congress calls a floor vote, issues a document, and then everyone goes to the same cafeteria for lunch.
Young women who work on Capitol Hill, this one's for you — they passed a whole resolution. It's framed now.
captionsJa: 下院は正式に「あなたの行いはダメです」と告げた。席もある。投票権もある。駐車場もある。でも告げた。
「非難決議」って、議会が「大変遺憾に思います」を公式書類にして手渡す儀式なんですよ。格式はある。効力はない。
超党派で可決。よかった。ただその超党派の合意が「これは起きた」というところで止まっている。
普通の会社ならHR案件。議会では本会議採決→書類手渡し→同じ食堂でランチ、というルートをたどる。
国会議事堂で働く若い女性のみなさん、決議が通りましたよ。額縁に入れてもらえます。
candidates.newsEn: The House of Representatives formally censured Republican Rep. Chuck Edwards of North Carolina following a House Ethics Committee investigation into allegations of unprofessional and inappropriate conduct toward two young female staffers. The censure vote drew bipartisan support. Edwards represents a district he has held since 2023.

ironyEn.contradiction: The House passed a bipartisan censure for workplace misconduct the same week it passed a bipartisan resolution condemning socialism — making 'harassment bad' and 'socialism bad' equally binding, which is to say, not at all.
ironyEn.absurdity: A censure in Congress means colleagues officially hand you a piece of paper saying you behaved badly, then immediately go back to working with you. It's less consequence than a one-star Yelp review.
ironyEn.outside: In most workplaces, the HR outcome here would look very different. In Congress, the outcome is a floor speech and a handshake from the other side of the aisle.

ironyEn.contradiction: The Ethics Committee called it 'unprofessional and inappropriate conduct.' The resolution passed. Edwards keeps his seat, his vote, and his parking space.
ironyEn.absurdity: Bipartisanship is rare in this Congress. When it showed up this week, it was to agree that harassing your young female staffers is, technically, not great.
ironyEn.outside: The censure is the legislative equivalent of a strongly worded email. It goes in the record. Nobody is required to act on it.

news.headline: Ed Markey, 80, Wins Massachusetts Democratic Primary Despite Age Challenges
news.summary: マサチューセッツ州選出の現職上院議員エド・マーキー（80歳）が、「マーキーは高齢で効果的でない」と訴えたセス・モールトン下院議員との民主党予備選を制し、再選に向けた党指名を勝ち取った。

commentary: 矛盾: 「若い世代に交代すべき」という主張を掲げた47歳の候補が、1976年から議員を続ける80歳に敗れた——民主党が世代交代を議論している最中の選挙で。
滑稽さ: マーキー氏が初当選した1976年、モールトン氏はまだ生まれていない。その相手に「古すぎる」と言って挑んで負けるというのは、ある種の完成された話になっている。
日本・海外から見ると: 日本でも「政治家の高齢化」は定番の議題だが、「高齢すぎる」を選挙の争点にして、その高齢候補に正面から負けるという展開は、どの国でも有権者の意思表示として面白い。
imagePrompts: An 80-year-old senator in a victory pose at a podium, confetti falling, campaign banner behind him reading 'FRESH IDEAS', while a significantly younger challenger looks on from the side
A campaign flyer split in two: left side reads 'TOO OLD TO BE EFFECTIVE' with a photo of an elderly senator; right side reads 'WINNER' with a check mark and the same photo
A timeline graphic on a wall showing '1976: Markey elected' and '1978: Opponent born' with a small arrow connecting them, displayed in a campaign headquarters
captions: Moulton's whole campaign was 'he's too old.' Markey's campaign was 'hold on, I'm still here.' Markey won.
Ed Markey was already in Congress when his opponent was born. That's not an attack line. That's just the calendar.
Democrats have been talking about generational change all year. Massachusetts said, 'Interesting. We'll revisit that in six years.'
At what age does a senator become too old? Massachusetts voters looked at 80, shrugged, and said, 'Not yet.'
Moulton lost on the argument that the other guy was too old. He's 47. I don't know what to do with that either.
captionsJa: モールトンの選挙戦略は「彼は年を取りすぎ」。マーキーの戦略は「まだここにいます」。マーキーが勝った。
マーキーが初めて議会に来た年、対立候補はまだ生まれていなかった。攻撃材料じゃなくて、ただのカレンダーの話。
民主党は今年ずっと「世代交代」を語ってきた。マサチューセッツは「面白い。6年後にまた考えよう」と答えた。
何歳になったら「年を取りすぎ」になるのか。マサチューセッツの有権者は80歳を見て「まだ」と言った。
「相手が古すぎる」という主張で負けたモールトンは47歳。私にもどう解釈すればいいかわからない。
candidates.newsEn: Senator Ed Markey, 80, won the Massachusetts Democratic primary on Tuesday, defeating Rep. Seth Moulton, 47, who had centered his campaign on the argument that the party needed younger leaders. The victory comes at a moment when Democrats nationally have been debating age and generational change in party leadership. Markey has served in Congress since 1976.

ironyEn.contradiction: Moulton ran a campaign built entirely on 'Markey is too old to be effective.' Markey won. The voters of Massachusetts looked at that argument and said, 'Sure, but have you considered: no.'
ironyEn.absurdity: Markey has been in Congress since 1976. Moulton was born in 1978. The 'too old' candidate won against someone who literally didn't exist yet when Markey first showed up to work.
ironyEn.outside: Democrats spent most of this election cycle arguing their party needed fresh faces. Massachusetts sent a message — just not that message.

ironyEn.contradiction: The centerpiece of Moulton's campaign was generational change. The outcome was: same generation, another term.
ironyEn.absurdity: At 80, Markey is old enough to remember when Massachusetts had a different senator. He outlasted that senator too.
ironyEn.outside: Globally, voters have shown they'll often back the familiar over the argument for change — even when the argument is literally about the age of the person they're backing.

news.headline: Homeland Security Chief Says ICE Could Be Deployed to Polling Places
news.summary: マークウェイン・マリン国土安全保障長官は、投票所に対する「脅威」や逮捕令状の執行が必要な場合、ICE（移民・関税執行局）捜査官を投票所に派遣する可能性があると述べた。

commentary: 矛盾: 「脅威があれば行く」という論理は一見合理的に聞こえるが、投票所に連邦移民捜査官が現れること自体が、多くの有権者にとって脅威になりうる——という構造的な矛盾を、発言は綺麗にスルーしている。
滑稽さ: 「投票を守るために捜査官を送る」という建前と、「捜査官が来ると投票に来ない人が出る」という現実が、同じ一文に共存している。民主主義の保護と抑制が、同じ手段で実現されようとしている。
日本・海外から見ると: 日本では投票所に警察官が常駐することはまずなく、投票率の低さは別の文脈で語られる。移民捜査官が投票所の周辺に立つという絵は、多くの民主主義国家では「選挙の健全性を示すもの」とは受け取られないだろう。
imagePrompts: A small-town polling place with a cheerful 'VOTE HERE' banner, staffed by elderly volunteers, while two ICE officers in tactical gear stand at the entrance checking clipboards
A Venn diagram with two overlapping circles: one labeled 'Protecting the vote', the other labeled 'Discouraging the vote' — the overlap is labeled 'ICE at polling places'
An 'OPEN FOR DEMOCRACY' sign on a polling place door, with a second, smaller sign below it reading 'Federal agents may be present', a lone voter hesitating at the sidewalk
captions: The polling place is safe, they said. Safe enough that we're sending armed federal immigration agents. Just in case.
Nothing gets voters excited to participate in democracy like finding out there might be ICE officers at the door. Very 'I Voted' sticker energy.
Their argument: ICE would only show up if there's a threat. Their blind spot: ICE showing up is the threat.
Most countries staff polling places with retirees and PTA volunteers. America is workshopping a different vibe.
Federal law bans intimidation at polls. Federal agents at polls is, per the secretary, totally different. He did not elaborate on what the difference is.
captionsJa: 投票所は安全です、と言った。だから連邦移民捜査官を送ります、とも言った。念のため。
玄関にICE捜査官がいるかもしれないと知ったとき、有権者の投票意欲がどう動くか——「参加したい」じゃないですよね。
「脅威があれば派遣する」という論理。盲点は、「ICEが来ること」が脅威だということ。
多くの国の投票所は、退職した教師や地域ボランティアで運営されている。アメリカは別の雰囲気を模索中。
連邦法は投票所での威圧を禁じている。投票所への連邦捜査官の派遣は、長官によれば別の話。どう違うかは説明されなかった。
candidates.newsEn: Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said Tuesday that ICE officers could be deployed to polling sites if there is a perceived threat to a polling place or if agents need to serve a warrant there. The comment drew immediate alarm from voting rights advocates and Democratic lawmakers, who warned it could suppress voter turnout. Federal law prohibits certain forms of intimidation at polling places.

ironyEn.contradiction: The plan is to protect the polling place by sending the people whose presence makes a large portion of the population afraid to approach the polling place.
ironyEn.absurdity: It's a voter protection strategy where the protection itself is the threat. Very efficient — one move does two jobs.
ironyEn.outside: International election observers are typically sent to countries to look for signs of voter intimidation. This is starting to sound like content for their reports.

ironyEn.contradiction: Mullin said ICE could show up 'if there is a threat.' The question left unanswered is who decides what counts as a threat, and whether ICE's presence automatically qualifies.
ironyEn.absurdity: Federal law already prohibits intimidation at polling places. The proposed solution to potential lawbreaking at polls is to add federal agents with arrest powers. Truly a belt-and-suspenders approach to democracy.
ironyEn.outside: Most democracies try to make polling places feel as unthreatening as possible — often staffing them with retired teachers and PTA volunteers. Just a different design philosophy.

news.headline: House Passes Resolution Condemning Socialism — With Voter ID Rider Tucked Inside
news.summary: 下院共和党は反社会主義を非難する決議を可決させたが、その中に物議を醸している有権者ID法案「SAVE America Act」の通過を求める条項を紛れ込ませていた。

commentary: 矛盾: 「社会主義を非難する」という象徴的な決議に、有権者ID法案の推進文言を抱き合わせで入れた構造がある。法的効力のない声明を、実際の立法意図の包み紙として使っている。
滑稽さ: 反社会主義決議なのに、中身を読むと選挙法の話が書いてある——という文書の二重構造が、「何について話しているのか」という問いに素直に答えていない。
日本・海外から見ると: 日本の国会でも予算案への抱き合わせ条項は議論になるが、「社会主義批判」と「選挙制度」を一枚の紙に同居させるという発想は、立法のパッケージングとして独特の大胆さがある。
imagePrompts: A large document labeled 'ANTI-SOCIALISM RESOLUTION' on the cover, held open to an interior page that reads 'Also: please pass our voter ID bill', a congressman smiling and pointing to the inside page
A matryoshka doll set: the outer doll labeled 'Condemning Socialism', opened to reveal a smaller doll labeled 'Voter ID Bill', opened to reveal a tiny doll labeled 'November Election'
A congressional podium with two signs: a large one reading 'DOWN WITH SOCIALISM' and a small sticky note below reading '(p.s. vote for our election bill)'
captions: They passed an anti-socialism resolution. Inside the anti-socialism resolution: a voter ID bill. Inside the voter ID bill: November.
Can't get your bill through on its own? Staple it to the thing everybody's already voting yes on. Congrats, you've invented legislative origami.
The resolution has no legal force. The rider has no legal force. But they are now both permanently in the Congressional Record, which is what counts as a win on a Tuesday in September.
Somewhere a staffer had to write 'WHEREAS socialism is bad' and then immediately write 'THEREFORE, voter ID.' That's the whole document. That person went home.
Other countries put policy riders in budget bills. America put one inside a vibe.
captionsJa: 反社会主義決議を通した。決議の中身を読んだら有権者ID法案が入っていた。そのさらに奥には11月がある。
単独では通せない法案は、みんながどうせ賛成する決議の中に入れればいい。立法折り紙の誕生。
この決議に法的効力はない。ライダーにも法的効力はない。でも議会議事録には残る。9月の火曜日の「勝ち」はそういうもの。
どこかのスタッフが「社会主義はよくない」と書いて、次の行に「だから有権者IDを」と書いた。それが書類の全部。その人は定時で帰った。
他の国は予算法案に政策を抱き合わせる。アメリカは「雰囲気」の中に入れた。
candidates.newsEn: The House passed a measure formally condemning socialism ahead of the November election. Republicans inserted language calling for the passage of the SAVE America Act — a highly controversial voter ID bill — into the same resolution. The socialism resolution is largely symbolic and has no binding legal effect.

ironyEn.contradiction: The resolution condemning socialism has no legal force. The voter ID language inserted inside it also has no legal force. Together they make a very official-sounding document that does nothing — but makes sure people read both sentences.
ironyEn.absurdity: Congress found a way to campaign and legislate at the same time while doing neither. It's a remarkably efficient use of a Tuesday.
ironyEn.outside: From the outside, watching a body with serious legislative powers spend floor time passing a symbolic anti-socialism statement — with a policy wish list stapled to the back — looks like a very elaborate press release.

ironyEn.contradiction: Republicans attached a voting bill to an anti-socialism resolution. The socialism resolution is symbolic. So the voting bill is now symbolically inside a symbol. Symbolism all the way down.
ironyEn.absurdity: The SAVE America Act is 'highly controversial,' which in this context means they couldn't pass it on its own, so they hid it inside the thing everyone would vote yes on.
ironyEn.outside: Legislative riders — slipping policy into unrelated bills — are common globally. Slipping policy into what is essentially a press release is a more advanced technique.

editorial.thread: 今日の5本を貫く糸：「建前」と「本音」が同じ一枚の紙に書いてある日。民主主義を守ると言いながら怖がらせる、社会主義を批判しながら別の議題を密輸する、「不適切」と書いた紙を渡してそのまま隣に座る。MapQuestだけが何も言わずに一番正直だった。
editorial.titleEn: MapQuest Beat ChatGPT. A Lake Did That.
editorial.subtitleEn: Five stories where the fine print is doing all the real work.
editorial.titleJa: 「反社会主義決議」の中に選挙法が入っていた話と、それより正直だったMapQuestの話
titleAltJa: 「社会主義を批判する紙」と「ICEが投票所に来るかもしれない話」が同じ週に出てきた
今週のアメリカを語るなら、もう言葉がない
editorial.leadJa:
「反社会主義決議」を開いたら中に選挙法が書いてありました。

議員は「不適切」と書いた紙を渡されて、翌日も同じ席に座っています。MapQuestが、湖の名前を変えなかっただけで今週のヒーローです。

アメリカ、今日もどうかしている。
editorial.introEn:
I want to talk about the fine print today. Not the fine print in contracts — I mean the fine print in democracy. The thing everyone agrees the document says, while quietly doing something else with it.

This week: MapQuest is No. 1 on the App Store, and it got there by doing absolutely nothing except not renaming a lake. Meanwhile, the House passed an anti-socialism resolution with a voter ID bill tucked inside it, like a prize in a cereal box. Also, ICE might show up at your polling place. To protect it, they say.

Here's your forecast: if you've ever felt like you were following the rules while people around you rewrote them mid-game, today's news is basically a mirror. That's not your fault. That's just Tuesday in September. You're fine.
editorial.introJa:
今日の話、全部「表の紙と裏の中身が違う」週なんですよ。

反社会主義決議を開いたら選挙法が入ってた。投票所を「守る」ためにICEを送るって言ってる。議員に「不適切」と書いた紙を渡して、翌日は隣に座って仕事してる。MapQuestは何も言わずに湖の名前を変えなかっただけで、今週のApp Store1位になった。

そんな5本です。

で、今日の占い。「なんか話がかみ合わないな」って感じてるとしたら、あなたがおかしいんじゃないと思う。書いてあることとやっていることが違う世界で、ちゃんと困惑してるだけだから。今日は、その困惑を笑っていい日です。
editorial.quipEn: This week, the most honest actor in American democracy was MapQuest. A mapping app from 2000. Which refused to rename a lake.
editorial.quipJa: 今週いちばん正直だったのは、MapQuestでした。
notesEn: MapQuest hit No. 1 on the App Store this week. It beat ChatGPT. Not by adding AI, not by redesigning the interface — by refusing to rename Lake Ontario to 'Lake America' after a Trump executive order. Google and Apple updated their maps. MapQuest did not. And apparently that's all it takes to become a hero in 2026.

The House passed an anti-socialism resolution this week. Symbolic, no legal force, everyone votes yes, done. Except — tucked inside the resolution was language pushing the SAVE America Act, a controversial voter ID bill. So the anti-socialism document was also, quietly, a voter ID document. The socialism was in the packaging.

Rep. Chuck Edwards was formally censured by the House this week for inappropriate conduct toward two female staffers. Bipartisan support. Official podium. Fancy ceremony. He still has his seat, his vote, and presumably his parking spot. A censure is Congress writing 'we are not pleased' in calligraphy and then going back to work.

Ed Markey is 80. He's been in Congress since 1976 — two years before his opponent, Rep. Seth Moulton, was born. Moulton's entire campaign was 'this guy is too old.' Markey won. That's not an attack line. That's just a calendar.

The Homeland Security Secretary said this week that ICE could be deployed to polling places if there's a threat there. Voting rights groups immediately pointed out that ICE showing up is the threat. The Secretary did not appear to find that confusing.
xJa: トランプ大統領令でオンタリオ湖が「レイク・アメリカ」に改名された。GoogleもAppleも従った。改名を拒否したのはMapQuestだった。MapQuestが今週App Store1位。2026年のことです。
下院が「反社会主義非難決議」を可決。中を読んだら選挙制度の話が書いてあった。反社会主義の紙に選挙法を忍ばせるの、立法の手品すぎる。
議員が若い女性スタッフへの不適切行為で「非難決議」を受けた。全会一致で可決。議員は翌日も同じ席で働いている。最大の処分が「紙を渡す」の制度、どうなってるんだ。
「高齢すぎる」を争点に47歳が挑み、80歳に負けた。80歳のマーキー議員が初当選した1976年、対立候補はまだ生まれていなかった。
「投票所に脅威があればICEを派遣する」と国土安全保障長官が発言。移民当局の捜査官が来ること自体が脅威だという指摘に、長官は特に応答しなかった。
raidEn: The part that gets me is that Google and Apple — trillion-dollar companies — updated their maps immediately. MapQuest, which most people thought was a screensaver by now, just didn't. And won.

A censure is Congress's way of saying 'we wrote your name on a list' and then going to lunch. The bipartisan part is honestly the funniest — they all agreed this was bad, and then agreed there was nothing to do about it.
Moulton's campaign slogan was basically 'he's old.' Markey's response was apparently just to show up and win. At 80. After 50 years in Congress. The timeline on this one is genuinely something.
The circular logic here is so clean: ICE at polling places protects voters. ICE at polling places scares voters away. Therefore, fewer voters to protect. Problem solved, technically.

The anti-socialism resolution is legally meaningless — it just says 'we don't like socialism.' Which is fine. But the voter ID bill they tucked inside is very much not meaningless. The wrapper was symbolic. The gift inside was not.
raidJa: MapQuestが何もしなかっただけで1位になるの、ちょっと笑ってしまいました。GoogleとAppleがすぐ従ったのと並べると、「どっちが体制に近いか」が完全に逆転してますよね。
「非難決議」が最大の処分という制度設計、改めて読んで驚きました。記事の「紙を渡して隣に座り続ける」という表現、まさにそうですよね。

反社会主義の紙に選挙法を同居させる発想、初めて読んだとき「え、本当に？」と思いました。立法のパッケージングとして、ちょっと唯一無二の大胆さがありますよね。
riffEn: Google has a market cap north of two trillion dollars. Apple is bigger. Between them, they have more engineers than most countries have voters. And when the executive order came down to rename Lake Ontario, both of them — immediately, quietly — updated their maps. MapQuest, which I genuinely thought had become a meme sometime around 2011, looked at that order and apparently said no. Not with a press release. Not with a lawsuit. Just by not doing it. And then it hit No. 1 on the App Store. Above ChatGPT. Because it refused to rename a lake. I'm not saying the big companies did something wrong. I'm just saying MapQuest is now the most punk thing in tech.

Here's how a censure works. The House investigates. The House votes. The House calls the member to the floor. Someone reads a document out loud that says, officially, on the record, that his behavior was unacceptable. He stands there. He receives this information. And then everyone goes back to their offices and continues to serve together in the same legislative body, with the same votes, the same staff budget, and presumably the same lunch options. The censure has no legal force. It cannot remove him. It cannot dock his pay. It is, to be precise, a piece of paper that says 'we noticed.' Which is more than nothing. But only just.

Seth Moulton is 47. He ran on the argument that Ed Markey, at 80, was simply too old to continue. This is a reasonable thing to argue. What is not reasonable — or rather, what is completely, perfectly, absurdly poetic — is that Markey has been in Congress since 1976. Moulton was born in 1978. So the man who ran against Markey for being too old was not yet alive when Markey started the job he is supposedly too old to continue. Moulton lost. The Democrats are still having their conversation about generational change. Massachusetts apparently decided to table it.

The secretary's argument, as best I can reconstruct it: polling places sometimes face threats, ICE officers respond to threats, therefore ICE officers might go to polling places. This is logical the same way a fire extinguisher is a source of water. Technically true. Deeply missing the point. Because the thing about sending federal immigration agents to a polling location — the specific detail that several people apparently had to explain out loud — is that federal immigration agents showing up is what makes a polling location feel threatening to a very large number of eligible voters. The protection and the suppression are the same object. You don't have to squint to see it.

They passed a resolution condemning socialism. Fine. Symbolic. Costs nothing, means nothing, everyone claps. But inside the anti-socialism resolution — tucked in, stapled, gift-wrapped — was language pushing the SAVE America Act, a voter ID bill that has been too controversial to pass on its own. So the document that officially says 'we oppose socialism' also, in the same breath, says 'pass this specific election legislation.' The outside of the package says one thing. The inside says something else entirely. Congress invented legislative origami, and they're very proud of the crane.

editorial.fullEn:
# MapQuest Beat ChatGPT. A Lake Did That.

## Today's Forecast

I want to talk about the fine print today. Not the fine print in contracts — I mean the fine print in democracy. The thing everyone agrees the document says, while quietly doing something else with it.

This week: MapQuest is No. 1 on the App Store, and it got there by doing absolutely nothing except not renaming a lake. Meanwhile, the House passed an anti-socialism resolution with a voter ID bill tucked inside it, like a prize in a cereal box. Also, ICE might show up at your polling place. To protect it, they say.

Here's your forecast: if you've ever felt like you were following the rules while people around you rewrote them mid-game, today's news is basically a mirror. That's not your fault. That's just Tuesday in September. You're fine.

---

## 1. MapQuest Hits No. 1 on App Store After Refusing to Rename Lake Ontario

*CBS News US — [source](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/mapquest-no-1-app-lake-ontario/)*

MapQuest, the once-dominant mapping service many had assumed was defunct, shot to the top of Apple's App Store free downloads chart after announcing it would keep traditional lake names rather than comply with a Trump executive order renaming Lake Ontario. The company's refusal placed it above ChatGPT on the charts. Google Maps and Apple Maps both updated their labels to reflect the new government-mandated name.

**Why It's Funny**

Google has a market cap north of two trillion dollars. Apple is bigger. Between them, they have more engineers than most countries have voters. And when the executive order came down to rename Lake Ontario, both of them — immediately, quietly — updated their maps. MapQuest, which I genuinely thought had become a meme sometime around 2011, looked at that order and apparently said no. Not with a press release. Not with a lawsuit. Just by not doing it. And then it hit No. 1 on the App Store. Above ChatGPT. Because it refused to rename a lake. I'm not saying the big companies did something wrong. I'm just saying MapQuest is now the most punk thing in tech.

**Say It Out Loud**

> MapQuest just beat ChatGPT on the charts. Not by being smarter. Not by being faster. By refusing to rename a lake.

---

## 2. House Censures Rep. Chuck Edwards for 'Inappropriate Conduct' Toward Female Aides

*CBS News US — [source](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/chuck-edwards-censure-vote-house-sexual-harassment/)*

The House of Representatives formally censured Republican Rep. Chuck Edwards of North Carolina following a House Ethics Committee investigation into allegations of unprofessional and inappropriate conduct toward two young female staffers. The censure vote drew bipartisan support. Edwards represents a district he has held since 2023.

**Why It's Funny**

Here's how a censure works. The House investigates. The House votes. The House calls the member to the floor. Someone reads a document out loud that says, officially, on the record, that his behavior was unacceptable. He stands there. He receives this information. And then everyone goes back to their offices and continues to serve together in the same legislative body, with the same votes, the same staff budget, and presumably the same lunch options. The censure has no legal force. It cannot remove him. It cannot dock his pay. It is, to be precise, a piece of paper that says 'we noticed.' Which is more than nothing. But only just.

**Say It Out Loud**

> Congress officially told him his behavior was unacceptable. He still has his desk. His vote. His parking spot. But they told him.

---

## 3. Ed Markey, 80, Wins Massachusetts Democratic Primary Despite Age Challenges

*The Guardian US — [source](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/sep/01/massachusetts-senate-democratic-primary)*

Senator Ed Markey, 80, won the Massachusetts Democratic primary on Tuesday, defeating Rep. Seth Moulton, 47, who had centered his campaign on the argument that the party needed younger leaders. The victory comes at a moment when Democrats nationally have been debating age and generational change in party leadership. Markey has served in Congress since 1976.

**Why It's Funny**

Seth Moulton is 47. He ran on the argument that Ed Markey, at 80, was simply too old to continue. This is a reasonable thing to argue. What is not reasonable — or rather, what is completely, perfectly, absurdly poetic — is that Markey has been in Congress since 1976. Moulton was born in 1978. So the man who ran against Markey for being too old was not yet alive when Markey started the job he is supposedly too old to continue. Moulton lost. The Democrats are still having their conversation about generational change. Massachusetts apparently decided to table it.

**Say It Out Loud**

> Moulton's whole campaign was 'he's too old.' Markey's campaign was 'hold on, I'm still here.' Markey won.

---

## 4. Homeland Security Chief Says ICE Could Be Deployed to Polling Places

*The Guardian US — [source](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/sep/01/trump-homeland-security-markwayne-mullin-polling)*

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said Tuesday that ICE officers could be deployed to polling sites if there is a perceived threat to a polling place or if agents need to serve a warrant there. The comment drew immediate alarm from voting rights advocates and Democratic lawmakers, who warned it could suppress voter turnout. Federal law prohibits certain forms of intimidation at polling places.

**Why It's Funny**

The secretary's argument, as best I can reconstruct it: polling places sometimes face threats, ICE officers respond to threats, therefore ICE officers might go to polling places. This is logical the same way a fire extinguisher is a source of water. Technically true. Deeply missing the point. Because the thing about sending federal immigration agents to a polling location — the specific detail that several people apparently had to explain out loud — is that federal immigration agents showing up is what makes a polling location feel threatening to a very large number of eligible voters. The protection and the suppression are the same object. You don't have to squint to see it.

**Say It Out Loud**

> The polling place is safe, they said. Safe enough that we're sending armed federal immigration agents. Just in case.

---

## 5. House Passes Resolution Condemning Socialism — With Voter ID Rider Tucked Inside

*CNBC Top News — [source](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/09/01/congress-vote-condemning-socialism-election.html)*

The House passed a measure formally condemning socialism ahead of the November election. Republicans inserted language calling for the passage of the SAVE America Act — a highly controversial voter ID bill — into the same resolution. The socialism resolution is largely symbolic and has no binding legal effect.

**Why It's Funny**

They passed a resolution condemning socialism. Fine. Symbolic. Costs nothing, means nothing, everyone claps. But inside the anti-socialism resolution — tucked in, stapled, gift-wrapped — was language pushing the SAVE America Act, a voter ID bill that has been too controversial to pass on its own. So the document that officially says 'we oppose socialism' also, in the same breath, says 'pass this specific election legislation.' The outside of the package says one thing. The inside says something else entirely. Congress invented legislative origami, and they're very proud of the crane.

**Say It Out Loud**

> They passed an anti-socialism resolution. Inside the anti-socialism resolution: a voter ID bill. Inside the voter ID bill: November.

---

## Today's Punchline

> This week, the most honest actor in American democracy was MapQuest. A mapping app from 2000. Which refused to rename a lake.
editorial.fullJa:
# 「反社会主義決議」の中に選挙法が入っていた話と、それより正直だったMapQuestの話

## 今日を占うよ〜

今日の話、全部「表の紙と裏の中身が違う」週なんですよ。

反社会主義決議を開いたら選挙法が入ってた。投票所を「守る」ためにICEを送るって言ってる。議員に「不適切」と書いた紙を渡して、翌日は隣に座って仕事してる。MapQuestは何も言わずに湖の名前を変えなかっただけで、今週のApp Store1位になった。

そんな5本です。

で、今日の占い。「なんか話がかみ合わないな」って感じてるとしたら、あなたがおかしいんじゃないと思う。書いてあることとやっていることが違う世界で、ちゃんと困惑してるだけだから。今日は、その困惑を笑っていい日です。

---

## 1. MapQuest Hits No. 1 on App Store After Refusing to Rename Lake Ontario

*CBS News US（[記事](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/mapquest-no-1-app-lake-ontario/)）*

トランプ大統領令に従ってGoogleとAppleがオンタリオ湖を「レイク・アメリカ」に改名する中、MapQuestが改名を拒否したことで話題となり、App Storeで無料アプリ1位に急浮上した。

**どこが笑える？**

Googleは時価総額が200兆円を超える会社で、Appleはもっと大きい。大統領令が来た日、両社はオンタリオ湖を「レイク・アメリカ」に書き換えた。素早く、静かに、特に抵抗なく。

MapQuestは、2000年代にほぼ化石になったと思っていた地図アプリなんですが、改名しなかった。声明も出さず、訴訟も起こさず、ただやらなかっただけ。それでApp Store1位になった。ChatGPTを抜いて。

誰が一番、湖に正直だったか。今週の答えは完全に出ています。

**このニュースをジョークにするなら...**

> MapQuestがApp StoreでChatGPTを抜いた。頭がいいから？いや。湖の名前を変えなかっただけ。

---

## 2. House Censures Rep. Chuck Edwards for 'Inappropriate Conduct' Toward Female Aides

*CBS News US（[記事](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/chuck-edwards-censure-vote-house-sexual-harassment/)）*

下院は倫理委員会の調査を受け、ノースカロライナ州選出の共和党議員チャック・エドワーズを、若い女性スタッフ2人への「不適切な行為」を理由に公式に非難決議した。

**どこが笑える？**

非難決議のしくみ、どんなものか。倫理委員会が調査して、下院が投票して、その議員を議場に呼んで、「あなたの行動は不適切でした」と書いた文書を読み上げる。議員はそれを受け取る。で、全員そのまま仕事に戻る。

同じ建物で、同じ票を持って、おそらく同じお昼を食べて。

法的効力はない。辞職も求めない。給与も止まらない。「私たちは気づきました」という紙を渡す、それが最大の処分。何もないよりはいい。でも、かなりギリギリのラインで「何もない」に近い。

**このニュースをジョークにするなら...**

> 下院は正式に「あなたの行いはダメです」と告げた。席もある。投票権もある。駐車場もある。でも告げた。

---

## 3. Ed Markey, 80, Wins Massachusetts Democratic Primary Despite Age Challenges

*The Guardian US（[記事](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/sep/01/massachusetts-senate-democratic-primary)）*

マサチューセッツ州選出の現職上院議員エド・マーキー（80歳）が、「マーキーは高齢で効果的でない」と訴えたセス・モールトン下院議員との民主党予備選を制し、再選に向けた党指名を勝ち取った。

**どこが笑える？**

モールトン議員、47歳。選挙戦の軸は「マーキーは80歳で高齢すぎる」でした。それ自体は真っ当な議論なんですが。

マーキーが議員になったのは1976年です。モールトンが生まれたのは1978年。つまり、「古すぎる」と言って挑んだ相手が、マーキーが初当選した時点でまだ生まれていなかった。

モールトンは負けました。民主党の世代交代論争、続いています。マサチューセッツは「引き続き検討します」という結論を出しました。

**このニュースをジョークにするなら...**

> モールトンの選挙戦略は「彼は年を取りすぎ」。マーキーの戦略は「まだここにいます」。マーキーが勝った。

---

## 4. Homeland Security Chief Says ICE Could Be Deployed to Polling Places

*The Guardian US（[記事](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/sep/01/trump-homeland-security-markwayne-mullin-polling)）*

マークウェイン・マリン国土安全保障長官は、投票所に対する「脅威」や逮捕令状の執行が必要な場合、ICE（移民・関税執行局）捜査官を投票所に派遣する可能性があると述べた。

**どこが笑える？**

マリン長官の論理、ちゃんと追うとこうです。投票所に脅威があればICEが行く。ICEは脅威に対処する。だから投票所にICEが来ることもある。

でも抜けているのは一つだけ。ICEが来ること自体が、多くの有権者にとっての脅威なんですよね。移民当局の捜査官が選挙当日に投票所の周りにいる——その絵が、投票に来ようとしていた人を家に帰らせる。

守る手段と、遠ざける手段が、まったく同じです。その指摘に、長官は特に何も言いませんでした。

**このニュースをジョークにするなら...**

> 投票所は安全です、と言った。だから連邦移民捜査官を送ります、とも言った。念のため。

---

## 5. House Passes Resolution Condemning Socialism — With Voter ID Rider Tucked Inside

*CNBC Top News（[記事](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/09/01/congress-vote-condemning-socialism-election.html)）*

下院共和党は反社会主義を非難する決議を可決させたが、その中に物議を醸している有権者ID法案「SAVE America Act」の通過を求める条項を紛れ込ませていた。

**どこが笑える？**

反社会主義非難決議、可決されました。象徴的な決議で、法的効力はゼロ。「社会主義はよくない」という公式声明みたいなものです。

で、その中身を読んだ人が気づいた。有権者ID法案「SAVE America Act」の通過を求める条項が、ちゃんと入っていた。

反社会主義の封筒を開けたら、選挙法が入っていた。封筒の外に書いてあることと、中に入っているものが全然違う。

これを「立法の折り紙」と呼ばずに何と呼べばいいのか、まだ言葉が見つかっていません。

**このニュースをジョークにするなら...**

> 反社会主義決議を通した。決議の中身を読んだら有権者ID法案が入っていた。そのさらに奥には11月がある。

---

## 今日のまとめジョーク/パンチライン

> 今週いちばん正直だったのは、MapQuestでした。

今日も読んでくれてありがとうございます。また明日の朝、ここで。
